Nuclear. The 2020 table let each Kazakh nuclear candidate build ten million MW a year from 2022, so ten gigawatts of it could appear in the first year of the run. Two per cent of the zone peak is about 230 MW a year in northern Kazakhstan, which is one 1200 MW unit every five years and the pace of a real nuclear programme; there is no floor, so a small system cannot build one at all. The first year is 2035: the October 2024 referendum approved a first plant at Ulken, Rosatom was selected in June 2025, and the commissioning date stated publicly is 2035-2036.

Coal and oil fired steam. Three per cent of the zone peak a year, never less than 300 MW, which is one supercritical unit a year in a system that can absorb one and one unit every few years in a system that cannot.
Combined cycle. The fastest thermal plant to build, so the highest rate: five per cent of the zone peak a year, never less than one 400 MW block.
Cogeneration. Slower than a pure power plant because it has to be built against a heat load, and the units are smaller: three per cent, floor 100 MW.
Open cycle gas turbine. Quick to build and modular: five per cent, floor 200 MW.
Reciprocating engines, the most modular machine in the table: five per cent, floor 100 MW.

Only the two Kazakh menu entries reach this row: every other hydro candidate is a named project, and a named project is not a menu entry, so the loop never asks this file about it. What a menu entry stands for is the small and medium hydro a country can add without a project attached to it, which is slow: two per cent of the zone peak a year, never less than 50 MW. The named projects sitting at zero capacity are listed in the manifest as an open question.
